questions.question: What are the six runtime shapes the lesson lists?
options: Request-response, streaming, durable execution, queue-based, event-driven, scheduled
Serverless, containerized, monolithic, microservice, edge-native, and hybrid deployment models
Celery, BullMQ, SQS plus Lambda, LangGraph, CrewAI Flows, and Claude Managed Agents stacks
Synchronous, asynchronous, batch, polling, webhook-triggered, and cron-triggered execution modes
questions.explanation: These are the six runtime shapes; pick a shape before picking a framework.

questions.question: When is request-response a poor fit?
options: On a 1-second classification task served synchronously through a single Agno or Mastra process
When the task takes longer than about 30 seconds and users hang up while workers pile up
On REST APIs that return within a single HTTP round trip without any streaming involved
On internal services where request and response happen inside the same process boundary
questions.explanation: Synchronous HTTP is only viable for short tasks; long tasks need queue/durable/event shapes.

questions.question: What is durable execution's core property?
options: Faster inference achieved by batching multiple concurrent agent requests together onto shared GPU hardware pools
Lower token cost achieved by trimming the context window after each tool call in the agent loop
State is checkpointed after every step so the runtime can resume from the last successful step on failure
Native voice support delivered through WebRTC streaming for progressive low-latency audio output
questions.explanation: Checkpoint-and-resume is the differentiator; LangGraph is the lesson's reference.

questions.question: Which Anthropic observation justifies queue-based runtimes for long-horizon agents?
options: Tasks always complete in under five seconds via a synchronous request-response API call
Tasks must run synchronously so the caller can retry immediately after a timeout
Cron-shaped scheduling alone solves long-horizon step counts without durable state
Computer use announcement: dozens-to-hundreds of steps per task is normal
questions.explanation: Anthropic flagged dozens-to-hundreds of steps per task as normal; that workload needs queues or durable runtimes.

questions.question: What does the lesson mean by 'observability is load-bearing'?
options: Without OTel GenAI spans and a Langfuse/Phoenix/Opik backend you cannot debug a multi-step agent that failed at step 40
Logs simply look prettier in a dashboard once OTel GenAI spans are wired into a Langfuse, Phoenix, or Opik backend for viewing
Disk usage grows large because every OTel GenAI span gets written out to a local log file on the host machine
Providers require OTel spans and trace export data for billing accuracy and rate-limit enforcement across API calls
questions.explanation: Observability is not optional for multi-step agents; it is the difference between debugging and replaying from scratch.

questions.question: Why must queue workers have a dead-letter queue (DLQ)?
options: DLQ is a mandatory feature required by AWS SQS
DLQ makes job processing run faster overall
Without DLQ, failed jobs vanish silently
DLQ encrypts job payloads at rest by default
questions.explanation: Failed jobs without DLQ disappear; DLQ is the parking lot for failed jobs.
